prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
# ARGUMENT

## The Class Cannot Be Certified Under Rule 23(b)(3) Because Individualized Damages Questions Will Overwhelm Any Common Questions.

### A. Plaintiffs bear the burden of proving predominance with evidence, not allegations.

Rule 23(b)(3) permits certification only if "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3). The predominance requirement is "far more demanding" than Rule 23(a)'s commonality requirement. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 34 (2013). Plaintiffs must prove each Rule 23 requirement by a preponderance of the evidence, and the district court must resolve the factual and legal disputes bearing on those requirements, even where they overlap with the merits. *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811, 815 (7th Cir. 2012); *Szabo v. Bridgeport Machs., Inc.*, 249 F.3d 672, 676–77 (7th Cir. 2001); *Am. Honda Motor Co. v. Allen*, 600 F.3d 813, 815–16 (7th Cir. 2010). Certification requires a "rigorous analysis," not deference to a plaintiff's assertion that common proof will suffice. *In re Pella Corp. Architect & Designer Series Windows Mktg., Sales Practices & Prods. Liab. Litig.*, 606 F.3d 391, 393–94 (7th Cir. 2010) (per curiam).

### B. Damages must be measurable on a classwide basis through a method tied to Plaintiffs' theory of liability.

*Comcast* holds that a damages model must measure only those damages attributable to the theory of liability on which the class is certified. 569 U.S. at 35. A model that cannot do so cannot establish that damages are capable of classwide measurement, and individual damages questions then predominate. *Id.* at 34–35. The Supreme Court has also rejected "Trial by Formula" shortcuts that would deprive a defendant of its right to litigate individualized defenses. *Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes*, 564 U.S. 338, 366–67 (2011).

This Court applies the same principles. In *Messner*, it affirmed the denial of certification, explaining that the predominance inquiry asks whether the need for individualized proof of injury and damages will swamp the common issues. 669 F.3d at 815, 817–19. In *Suchanek v. Sturm Foods, Inc.*, 764 F.3d 750, 759–61 (7th Cir. 2014), it reversed a certification order because whether each class member was injured, and in what amount, turned on individual circumstances. Common questions about the defendant's conduct could not carry the class when each member's recovery would require a separate inquiry.

### C. Plaintiffs' damages theory fails this standard.

Plaintiffs identify common questions about Defendant's alleged conduct. But the damages each putative class member could recover depends on facts unique to that member. [Insert record cites: e.g., differing purchase prices, usage, mitigation, offsetting benefits, and causation.] Plaintiffs have proposed no model that measures those damages by common proof. Their expert's methodology [does not isolate damages attributable to the liability theory / relies on averages that mask material variation among members]. Under *Comcast*, that failure is dispositive. 569 U.S. at 35–38.

### D. Plaintiffs' anticipated authorities do not rescue certification.

Plaintiffs will invoke the rule that the need for individual damages calculations does not, standing alone, defeat certification. *Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 801 (7th Cir. 2013); *Chi. Teachers Union, Local No. 1 v. Bd. of Educ.*, 797 F.3d 426, 444 (7th Cir. 2015). Defendant does not contend otherwise. Those decisions permit certification where liability can be established through common proof and damages can be computed by a mechanical or formulaic method. In *Butler*, the court emphasized that the common questions of defect and liability were substantial and that remaining damages issues could be handled through separate proceedings or subclasses. 727 F.3d at 801–02.

This case is different. Here, individualized issues bear not only on the amount of damages but also on injury, causation, and defenses, and Plaintiffs offer no common method to resolve them. Where individual inquiries of that kind would dominate the litigation, *Butler* does not apply. *See Suchanek*, 764 F.3d at 760–61; *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815–19. Nor may Plaintiffs avoid the problem by promising to sort out damages after certification. Rule 23 requires that predominance be established at the certification stage. *Szabo*, 249 F.3d at 676–77; *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 811.

### E. Issue certification or subclassing would not cure the defect.

Plaintiffs cannot rely on Rule 23(c)(4) to salvage the class. Carving out liability issues for classwide treatment would leave thousands of individual damages trials, with the same evidence presented repeatedly and with serious Seventh Amendment risks. That outcome would defeat the efficiencies Rule 23(b)(3) is designed to achieve. The district court therefore abused its discretion in certifying the class, and the order should be reversed.
